name: intercepting-filter
intent: Wrap the core request handler with an ordered, configurable chain of independent filters, so cross-cutting pre- and post-processing can be added, removed or reordered without editing the handler.
problem: Cross-cutting pre/post processing must wrap the core handler: authentication, session checks, logging, encoding and compression are needed around many requests, and hard-wiring them as nested conditionals inside the handler makes the flow rigid and copies the same checks into every endpoint.
context: Server-side request/response processing (a web presentation tier or an RPC boundary) where the same concerns apply to many endpoints, where the set and order of concerns must vary per route or per deployment, and where a container or framework can own the construction and traversal of the chain.
benefits: Each cross-cutting concern lives in exactly one component and is reused wherever it is mapped, instead of being repeated or nested inside handler code.
Filters are added, removed, reordered or reconfigured declaratively (deployment descriptor, startup pipeline, routing table) without touching the target.
Pre- and post-processing are both available from a single component: a filter runs code before delegating and can transform or inspect the response after the rest of the chain returns.
Short-circuiting is first-class: a filter that rejects a request (authentication, rate limit, size cap) returns a response and skips the remaining filters and the target.
Centralised enforcement points make security and observability policies auditable, because the check is a named component rather than scattered conditionals.
Each filter is a small unit with a single responsibility and can be tested in isolation from the target.
tradeoffs: Execution order is the pattern's real contract: filters that depend on an earlier filter's side effects create invisible coupling that breaks as soon as the chain is reconfigured.
Indirection: the request no longer shows which component produced a response, so debugging means reconstructing chain order from configuration.
Every request traverses the whole chain, and frameworks that wrap the request/response object add an allocation per layer.
Declarative registration drifts from the code: a filter can be present but unmapped, and quietly never run.
Failure modes get subtle - a filter that swallows exceptions or forgets to delegate hangs or silently short-circuits the request.
Filters with mutable instance state turn into concurrency bugs, because most container or framework instances are shared across requests.
The mechanism belongs to the platform (servlet container, framework pipeline), so the design does not port unchanged to another stack.

participants.responsibility: Builds the chain with the filters mapped to the requested target, in the configured order, and initiates processing.
Ordered collection of independent filters that coordinates traversal, passing request, response and control to the next filter and finally to the target.
One pluggable component that performs a single pre- and/or post-processing concern and decides whether to delegate or short-circuit.
The core resource requested by the client (handler, controller, servlet, RPC method) that performs the application work and is unaware of the filters around it.
Initiates the request that enters the chain and receives the filtered response.

use_cases: Authentication, session and CSRF gates in front of every protected endpoint (servlet filters, Spring HandlerInterceptor, Vapor middleware).
Request logging, correlation-ID assignment, metrics and tracing wrappers around handlers (Express middleware, Ktor Monitoring phase, ASP.NET Core middleware).
Response-path transformation: compression, encoding conversion and header injection (httpd output filters, servlet response wrappers, Rack body wrappers).
Input sanitisation, payload size limits and content-type validation applied uniformly instead of per endpoint.
Rate limiting, IP allow-listing and audit trails as deployment-mapped filters that can short-circuit before the target runs.
Cross-cutting RPC concerns - metadata handling, server-side auth, fault injection, caching - as gRPC interceptors or tower layers.
Conditional-GET and caching filters that answer the request from a cache and skip the target entirely.
API Gateway request/response transformation: header manipulation, routing rewrites, and protocol translation as gateway-level filters (AWS API Gateway, Kong, Envoy proxy).
GraphQL middleware for field-level authorization, query depth limiting, and request batching via DataLoader pattern.
Serverless cold-start validation: validate API keys, JWT claims, and payload schemas before invoking the actual function handler.
WebSocket pipeline filters for per-message authentication, rate limiting, and protocol upgrade validation.
CDN edge functions and VCL (Varnish Configuration Language) that intercept requests at the CDN layer for rewrite, redirect, or caching decisions.

Java Servlet Filter chains (for example in servlet containers) apply authentication, request wrapping, compression or audit logic before and after a mapped resource through Filter.doFilter and FilterChain.doFilter.
ASP.NET Core middleware pipelines compose request delegates with Use, Run and Map so logging, authentication, branching and terminal short-circuits can surround endpoint execution.
Express application and router middleware mounted with app.use() run in registration order, enabling route-scoped guards, request enrichment, response handling and explicit next() short-circuits.
avoid_when: A single handler needs one extra check: call a helper function inside it - a chain of one is pure indirection.
The concern is not request/response shaped (validating an object graph): use Decorator, Specification or a plain service instead.
The framework already offers a middleware or filter mechanism: configure that one rather than building a second, hand-rolled chain beside it.
The set and order of concerns are fixed and tiny: a straight-line function is easier to read than a chain nobody can see at once.
Only one of pre- or post-processing is needed and the language composes functions: a single wrapping function suffices.
The processing needs rich per-endpoint typed input and framework filter hooks only expose an untyped request; keep the logic in the handler or a typed decorator.
anti_patterns: Filters that implement domain or business logic and reach into application services, turning the chain into a hidden controller.
Order-dependent filters with undocumented mutual assumptions (filter A writes the attribute filter B reads), so a reordering breaks behaviour silently.
Filter soup: dozens of one-line filters whose combined effect nobody can reconstruct from the configuration.
Authorization as just another filter that a new route mapping forgets to include - an unguarded endpoint created by configuration drift.
Filters that catch and swallow exceptions, or answer 200 on failure, so faults disappear from the response.
Stateful filters that store per-request data in instance fields of a component shared by all requests.
Calling next() after the response has started, causing protocol violations or corrupted response bodies.
Filters registered in the wrong order that perform expensive work (database lookups, external API calls) before a short-circuiting auth filter can reject the request.
Middleware that modifies the request object in-place without creating a wrapper, polluting subsequent filters with mutated state.
Async filters that forget to await the chain-proceed call, silently short-circuiting the remainder of the chain.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: one component per cross-cutting concern, so the target keeps only application logic.
Open/closed principle: new processing is added by registering a filter, not by editing the target or the existing filters.
Single responsibility per filter, and composition over inheritance - filters wrap the chain instead of subclassing the handler.
Chain order is an explicit interface contract: filters communicate through the declared request context, never through implicit sequencing.
Dependency inversion: the chain depends on the filter abstraction, and the target does not know that filters exist.
best_practices: Declare registration and order in one place (deployment descriptor, pipeline configuration, routing table) and review it like any other interface.
Keep filters stateless; put per-request data into the request or a context object.
Let a filter either delegate or short-circuit — never delegate after the response body has been written, and never swallow exceptions silently.
Put cheap rejections (authentication, rate limit, size cap) early so expensive work never starts for a request that will be refused.
Test each filter in isolation and the assembled chain as a whole (order effects and short-circuit paths).
Keep the chain short: fold trivial filters together, and reserve the mechanism for genuinely cross-cutting concerns.
Document what each filter requires and what it adds to the request, because those attributes are the chain's real interface.
Place exception-handling filters first in the chain so they catch exceptions from all downstream filters and the target.
In async pipelines, prefer async/await filter variants to avoid blocking the thread pool; ensure the chain-proceed call is awaited.
Release resources in finally blocks or use try-with-resources; filters hold connections or memory that must be returned regardless of success or failure.
Configure filters via dependency injection or a descriptor (not hardcoded class names) so deployment teams can reorder without recompiling.
For response-body filters, set headers before the first byte is written; check HttpResponse.HasStarted before mutating headers.
In multi-tenant or multi-tenant SaaS contexts, put tenant-resolution filters before any tenant-specific authorization filter.
sources: Alur, Crupi & Malks, Core J2EE Patterns: Best Practices and Design Strategies (2001/2003) - Intercepting Filter (presentation tier): pluggable filters intercept incoming requests and outgoing responses, are configured declaratively, and wrap the target resource.

Oracle Java EE 7 Specification: javax.servlet.Filter interface (Servlet 2.3+) — defines the canonical contract for request/response filtering with doFilter(), init(FilterConfig), and destroy(), including recommended use cases (authentication, logging, compression, encryption, XSL/T).

Oracle Java EE 7 Specification: javax.servlet.FilterChain interface — defines the chain-proceed contract where FilterChain.doFilter() invokes the next filter or the target resource at the end of the chain.

Microsoft Learn: ASP.NET Core Middleware — documents the .NET pipeline model with Use(), Run(), Map(), short-circuiting terminal middleware, and the importance of exception-handling middleware being registered early.

Express.js Documentation: Using Middleware — covers application-level, router-level, error-handling, built-in, and third-party middleware; documents next() calling convention and the hanging-request hazard when next() is not called.

PEP 3333 (Python Web Server Gateway Interface v1.0.1): defines WSGI middleware as components that play both sides (application to server, server to application), enabling layered filter chains in Python web frameworks.

Spring Security Reference: Servlet Architecture — documents FilterChainProxy, SecurityFilterChain, DelegatingFilterProxy, and the critical importance of filter ordering (exploit protection → authentication → authorization).

Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (PoEAA, 2002): documents Intercepting Filter alongside Front Controller and Page Controller, noting that Intercepting Filter is the J2EE-pattern name for what is essentially a specialized Chain of Responsibility for the presentation tier.
